title: AI helped build BooDash. A player on a bus exposed what our control tests missed.
author: Training_Relation_89
selftext:
We're the Shapemo / MetaLeap team making BooDash, a small Halloween action game. AI assists our code, character graphics and text. The in-game reactions follow authored rules; there is no live model or character chatbot.



A useful lesson from testing: passing input tests didn't mean the controls fit someone's actual situation. A Reddit player wanted to play one-handed on a phone while riding a bus. Our original two-sided layout made that awkward. The Web version now offers left- or right-handed controls, with movement centered in the chosen control area and a drag-to-target skill that confirms on release. We've followed up with that player; we don't yet have their verdict on the change.



That has become our development loop: real play -> one concrete problem -> a scoped change -> replay the same situation. We also reject gameplay clips that technically work but lack a readable threat, a response and a complete ending. The attached Pip run shows the Pumpkin King's charge warning, the dodge and the opening to counterattack. It's normal gameplay with original game audio; observation pauses are removed, without changing action order, speed, score or difficulty.



Try the free browser demo, levels 1–9, without a download or game account: [https://games.shapemo.com/play/boodash/](https://games.shapemo.com/play/boodash/)



If you try it on a phone, can you move and aim a skill comfortably with one hand? For other AI-assisted developers: which real play situation found a problem your automated checks missed?
